title: The third interruption
subtitle: Active listening when the room is moving too fast
role: You are the team leader, responsible for making sure everyone in the room is actually heard.
hook:
Active listening is easy to agree with and hard to do at eleven minutes past the hour with a decision to make.

One of your team has stopped speaking in meetings. She has not complained, her work is good, and nobody else has noticed. What happens next is yours.

principles.title: Notice the withdrawal, not just the interruption
principles.summary: The moment that matters is when someone stops trying, and it is almost always quiet.
principles.example: "You went quiet after Dan cut in — what were you going to say?"
principles.pitfall: Moving the meeting on because nobody objected, which reads as agreement and is usually just people giving up.

principles.title: Describe behaviour, not character
principles.summary: A person can act on "three times on Thursday". Nobody can act on "you're a poor listener".
principles.example: "You spoke over Priya three times on Thursday" rather than "you dominate meetings".
principles.pitfall: Softening it into a character note — "you can be a bit much" — which cannot be acted on and is heard as an insult.

principles.title: A workaround is a decision
principles.summary: Accommodating a problem without naming its cost is how the accommodation becomes permanent.
principles.example: "We can work around it this week, and here is what that costs us if it becomes the norm."
principles.pitfall: Quietly absorbing the extra work to keep the peace, which turns a temporary fix into the way things are done.

nodes.title: The third interruption
nodes.situation:
Thursday stand-up, eleven minutes in. Priya has started the same sentence three times. Each time, Dan has finished it for her — faster, louder, and not quite right.

She stops trying. She looks at her notes and says, "It's fine, go on."

The room moves on. Nobody else appears to have noticed.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: Right, so we're agreed on the Friday cutover?
nodes.challenge: Priya has just withdrawn from the conversation. What do you do?

choices.text: Stop the room. "Priya, you started to say something three times. I'd like to hear it."
choices.consequence: The room goes quiet in a way that is slightly uncomfortable. Priya hesitates, then says the cutover date collides with the audit. Dan opens his mouth and closes it again.
choices.feedback: You made the withdrawal visible without making anyone the villain. Naming what you observed — three attempts — is harder to dismiss than "let Priya speak".
choices.outcomenote: The best of the three, and the only one that costs you anything at the time: four awkward seconds while the room waits. Naming what you saw, in the moment, is what makes the interruption a fact rather than an accusation - and it is the only version Priya can build on, because it happens in front of the people who were doing it. She learns that the room will hold still for her, which is what makes her speak up on Friday without being invited.

choices.text: Make a note to catch Priya afterwards, and let the meeting run.
choices.consequence: The meeting finishes on time. You catch Priya at her desk at four. She tells you about the audit collision, and adds that she'd mentioned it twice already.
choices.feedback: You did follow up, which matters. But the decision was made without her information, and the room learned that being talked over is survivable rather than something that gets corrected.
choices.outcomenote: The plausible middle, and the one that quietly teaches the wrong thing. You do hear her, which is why it feels like listening - but you hear her alone, at four o'clock, away from the people who needed to. The meeting learns nothing, Dan learns nothing, and Priya learns that her input reaches you through a side channel. The next time she has something, she will wait for the side channel.

choices.text: Say "let's keep it moving" and confirm the Friday date.
choices.consequence: The stand-up ends four minutes early. On Friday the cutover runs into the audit window and is rolled back at 6pm.
choices.feedback: The information you needed was in the room and had tried to reach you three times. Speed here cost a weekend.
choices.outcomenote: The most expensive of the three, and it looks like efficiency. Four minutes saved against a rollback: the cost is not the meeting, it is the information that was in the room and left it unsaid. Priya now has evidence that starting a sentence here is not worth finishing, and the next time she will not start it.

nodes.title: What Priya actually said
nodes.situation:
Priya lays it out in about ninety seconds: the cutover window overlaps the external audit, the auditors need read access to the same system, and she flagged it in the channel on Monday.

Dan says, "I didn't see that." He isn't being defensive. He genuinely didn't.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: I didn't see that. Sorry — go on.

nodes.title: The pattern repeats
nodes.situation:
Two weeks later, same meeting, same shape. Priya contributes once at the start and then stops. When you ask her directly for a view, she says "whatever the team thinks".

Dan is not hostile. He is quick, and he fills silence. The gap between those two things has become a pattern nobody has named.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: Whatever the team thinks is fine by me.

nodes.title: Dan, one to one
nodes.situation:
You've asked Dan for fifteen minutes. He arrives cheerful and slightly puzzled.

He is one of the most useful people on the team. He is also the reason one of the others has stopped speaking, and he has no idea.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: What's up? Everything alright with the cutover?

choices.text: Describe what you saw, not what it meant. "In Thursday's stand-up, Priya began three times and each time the sentence got finished for her."
choices.consequence: Dan sits back. "Three times?" He thinks about it. "I do that. My wife says I do that." He asks what he should do instead, and means it.
choices.feedback: Observable behaviour is something a person can accept without having to defend their character. "You talk over people" invites an argument about whether that is true. "Three times on Thursday" does not.
choices.outcomenote: The best available, because it gives Dan something he can act on. A behaviour, a time and a count are checkable - he can disagree with them, which is exactly why he believes them. The discomfort is his own recognition rather than your verdict, and that is the difference between a person who agrees with you and a person who changes.

choices.text: Ask how he thinks the stand-ups are going.
choices.consequence: "Good?" he says. "Bit long maybe." You end up steering the conversation round to interrupting anyway, but from further away, and he leaves not quite sure whether he was in trouble.
choices.feedback: The open question is a reasonable instinct and sometimes it works. Here it asked Dan to guess what you had already decided to tell him, which is a slower route to the same place and leaves the message blurred.
choices.outcomenote: The gentle opening that costs the conversation its point. Asking how it is going invites him to answer about the meeting rather than about himself, so you spend the time steering back to the thing you could have said first. He leaves knowing you wanted something and not what it was.

choices.text: Tell him he needs to be more aware of how he comes across.
choices.consequence: Dan agrees immediately and warmly, and nothing changes, because he has no idea which behaviour you are describing. At the next stand-up he interrupts Priya twice.
choices.feedback: Feedback that names a quality rather than an action cannot be acted on. He would have fixed it if he had known what "it" was.
choices.outcomenote: The worst of the three, and the one that produces the warmest response. 'How you come across' names no behaviour, so there is nothing to stop doing. He agrees because agreeing is easy and costs him nothing, and you both leave believing the conversation worked. Nothing changes, and the next one is harder because this one apparently went fine.

nodes.title: He asks for the rule
nodes.situation:
"Just tell me what to do," Dan says. "I'm not going to notice in the moment. I never do."

It is a fair request. He is asking for a mechanism, not a lecture.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: Just tell me what to do. I won't notice on my own.
nodes.continuelabel: Think about what would actually work

nodes.title: Nothing changes on its own
nodes.situation:
The next stand-up runs exactly as the last one did. Whatever was said in that room, it did not survive contact with a live meeting and a tight agenda.

Priya has started sending her points to you by message beforehand, so that they get made.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: I'll just send it to you before, easier that way.
nodes.continuelabel: Notice what she has started doing

nodes.title: Nothing to act on
nodes.situation:
Dan is friendly with you all week, and the stand-ups run exactly as they did. He has nothing to stop doing, because you did not name anything he does.

On Thursday he mentions, lightly, that he has been "trying to be more aware". Priya says nothing at all.
nodes.imageprompt: A stand-up meeting where one person is talking and another is looking at the table, not speaking
nodes.imagealt: A team meeting where one person listens without contributing

nodes.title: The workaround, with Dan in the room
nodes.situation:
Priya starts sending you the updates the night before instead of raising them. They are excellent, and the meeting runs smoothly on them.

On Thursday she says it out loud, in front of everyone: "I just send them to you now, it is easier." Dan looks up.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: It's honestly easier this way. I don't mind.
nodes.challenge: She has said it in the room. What do you do with that?

choices.text: Take it seriously in front of everyone. "That is a workaround, and it is working. What I want to know is what we are working around."
choices.consequence: The table goes quiet for a second. Dan says, "Is it me?" Priya does not answer, which is an answer. Dan says he will leave a gap after she starts.
choices.feedback: Naming the workaround in the room let the person causing it ask the question himself, which is the only version he will act on.
choices.outcomenote: The best of the three, and the most uncomfortable for about four seconds. She raised it publicly, so answering privately would tell her she was wrong to. Asking what the workaround is FOR puts the question in the room without naming anybody, and Dan gets to arrive at it himself - which is why he does something about it.

choices.text: Thank her and say you will pick it up with her afterwards.
choices.consequence: You do pick it up, at four. She is friendly about it and nothing changes. The messages keep arriving and the room stays quiet.
choices.feedback: Moving a public problem into a private conversation solves it for one person and leaves it in place for the room.
choices.outcomenote: The plausible middle, and it looks like discretion. She raised it in front of everyone, which was the brave part; taking it out of the room hands the privacy back to the person who did not need it. Nothing is refused and nothing changes.

choices.text: Say it is working well and move on to the next item.
choices.consequence: The meeting runs four minutes early. Priya sends the next update that evening, and the one after. She does not raise anything in the room again.
choices.feedback: Endorsing the workaround in front of the team makes it the way things are done here.
choices.outcomenote: The worst, and it costs nothing in the moment, which is what makes it easy. Calling the workaround "working" in front of everybody promotes it from something she does to how this team operates - and the next person to join learns it by watching.

nodes.imageprompt: A stand-up meeting where one person has just said something that made the others look up
nodes.imagealt: A team meeting where a comment has just landed

nodes.title: The workaround
nodes.situation:
Priya's messages are excellent. They arrive the night before, they are clear, and they mean the meeting runs smoothly.

They also mean she has stopped speaking in the room, and that the team now hears her points in your voice rather than hers.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: It's honestly easier this way. I don't mind.
nodes.challenge: She says she doesn't mind. Do you accept the workaround?

choices.text: Name the cost. "It works, and I'll keep reading them. But the team is hearing your thinking in my voice, and that's a loss for you and for them."
choices.consequence: Priya is quiet for a moment. "I hadn't thought about the second part." She agrees to try making one point herself each stand-up, and asks you not to rescue her if it goes badly.
choices.feedback: You took her stated preference seriously and still said the thing she hadn't considered. Accepting a workaround without naming its cost is how a temporary accommodation becomes permanent.
choices.outcomenote: The best of the three: it accepts the workaround and still names what it costs. Priya is not being asked to stop protecting herself, she is being shown the second half of the picture - that a private channel works for her and hides the problem from everyone else. She had not thought about the second part, which is the point: you cannot decide about a cost nobody has said out loud.

choices.text: Thank her and keep the arrangement, but resolve to keep an eye on it.
choices.consequence: The arrangement holds. Three months later she is still sending messages, and a new starter has quietly copied the habit.
choices.feedback: Nothing here is wrong, exactly. But "keep an eye on it" is not a mechanism, and the pattern had already shown it could outlast your attention.
choices.outcomenote: The comfortable one, and it works for three months, which is what makes it hard to argue with. But 'keeping an eye on it' is a decision to do nothing with a plan attached, and the arrangement hardens into how things are done here. By the time a new starter has copied it, it is not a workaround any more - it is the process.

choices.text: Take her at her word. She said she doesn't mind.
choices.consequence: She doesn't raise it again. At her next review she asks about roles on other teams, and mentions she'd like somewhere she can "contribute more directly".
choices.feedback: Taking someone at their word sounds respectful. Here it meant accepting the first answer from a person who had already learned that the room does not hold space for her second one.
choices.outcomenote: The worst, and it is worst precisely because she gave you permission. 'I don't mind' is what people say about a cost they have decided to absorb; taking it at face value moves that cost permanently onto her. She stops raising it, and the next thing you hear about it is her asking what roles are open on other teams.

nodes.title: The mechanism
nodes.situation: Whatever you do next has to survive a tight agenda, a loud colleague and your own attention on a bad week. It has to work when you are not thinking about it.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: So how are we doing this?
nodes.challenge: What do you put in place?

choices.text: Change the format: each person gets ninety uninterrupted seconds, in a fixed order, before any discussion.
choices.consequence: The first two stand-ups are stilted and everyone hates it. By the fourth, Dan is timing himself and Priya has stopped pre-writing. The format holds because it does not depend on anyone remembering to be considerate.
choices.feedback: A structural change survives a bad week. It also spreads the cost across everyone instead of asking one person to be braver and another to be quieter.
choices.outcomenote: The best available, and the only one that does not depend on anybody remembering. Everyone hates the first fortnight, which is the honest price of a structural fix: it changes what the meeting IS rather than asking people to be better at the meeting they already have. By the fourth week Dan is timing himself, which is a habit rather than a favour.

choices.text: Ask Dan to let Priya finish, and ask Priya to push back if he doesn't.
choices.consequence: It works when both of them remember. Dan remembers about half the time. Priya pushes back once, early, and not again.
choices.feedback: You asked two people to change behaviour in the moment, which is the hardest place to change it, and you put the harder half on the person with less room to spend.
choices.outcomenote: The reasonable one, and it puts the work on the two people least able to do it. Dan has to remember something he does without noticing, and Priya has to interrupt the person who interrupts her. It holds when both of them are at their best, which is not what a mechanism is for.

choices.text: Say you'll watch for it and step in when it happens.
choices.consequence: You step in twice in the first week, once in the third, and then a release slips and you stop noticing entirely.
choices.feedback: Your attention is the scarcest resource in the room and the first thing a busy week takes. A rule that depends on it is a rule that works until it matters.
choices.outcomenote: The worst, because it makes you the mechanism. It works while you are watching and stops the first week you are busy - and a release always comes. Worse, the team learns that the rule is your attention rather than the meeting's shape, so when your attention goes, so does the rule.

nodes.title: It has become how things are done
nodes.situation:
A new starter joined three weeks ago. This morning she sends you her update the night before the stand-up, formatted exactly like Priya's.

She has never raised anything in the room. Nobody told her not to. She simply copied what she saw working.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: This is how it works here, right?
nodes.challenge: The workaround has been learnt by somebody who was never part of it. What do you do?

choices.text: Change the format for everyone: ninety uninterrupted seconds each, in a fixed order.
choices.consequence: The first two stand-ups are stilted and everyone hates it. By the fourth, the new starter raises something nobody else had noticed.
choices.feedback: A rule that lives in the structure does not depend on anyone remembering to be good at it.
choices.outcomenote: The best available, and the only one that reaches somebody who was never part of the original problem. She copied what she saw; changing what there is to see is the only correction that works on a person who did nothing wrong.

choices.text: Tell the new starter she is welcome to raise things in the stand-up.
choices.consequence: She says "of course" and keeps sending the messages. She has watched what happens to people who speak in this meeting.
choices.feedback: Permission does not undo a demonstration.
choices.outcomenote: It is true, it is kind, and it is not what she is going on. She has watched a room for three weeks and drawn a conclusion; being told the opposite once does not outweigh that. Permission is not evidence.

choices.text: Leave it. The updates are good and the meetings are efficient.
choices.consequence: The meetings stay efficient. Six months later the stand-up is four people confirming what you already read the night before.
choices.feedback: An efficient meeting where nobody says anything new is a meeting that could be an email, and it is now the only place the team meets.
choices.outcomenote: The worst, and it will feel like the right call for months. What you are left with is a meeting that runs on time because nothing happens in it, and a team whose thinking you only ever meet in writing, one person at a time.

nodes.imageprompt: A new team member at a desk composing a written message rather than speaking to the people nearby
nodes.imagealt: A new team member writing a message instead of speaking

nodes.title: Six weeks on
nodes.situation:
Priya raises a risk in the stand-up — unprompted, in the room, and she holds the floor while she explains it. Dan waits, then builds on it.

Afterwards Priya asks you, not unkindly, why it took six weeks.
nodes.facilitatorspeech: Why did that take six weeks?
nodes.challenge: It is a real question and it deserves a real answer.

choices.text: "Because I watched it happen for a while before I did anything, and that was mine to fix sooner."
choices.consequence: She nods. "Alright." That is the whole conversation, and it is enough. She raises something else the following week without checking whether it is safe to.
choices.feedback: Naming your own delay without performing guilt about it is what makes the correction credible. She was not asking for an apology; she was asking whether you had seen it.
choices.outcomenote: The best of the three, and the shortest. She asked a real question and this is a real answer: you watched, you were slow, and you are saying so without turning it into an apology she then has to manage. 'Alright' is what being levelled with sounds like, and it is why she brings you the next thing two weeks later.

choices.text: "These things take time to shift."
choices.consequence: She says "sure" and goes back to her desk. The format holds, and she keeps using it, but she does not ask you a question like that again.
choices.feedback: It is true and it is also the answer that costs you nothing. She had noticed something real and offered you the chance to confirm it.
choices.outcomenote: The line that closes a conversation without answering it. It is not untrue, and that is the trouble - it explains the delay as a property of the world rather than a choice you made. She says 'sure' because there is nothing to say to it. The format holds; the door does not open.

choices.text: "Well, you could have said something earlier too."
choices.consequence: The conversation ends politely. Her points continue to arrive in the stand-up, correctly and briefly, and nothing else does.
choices.feedback: The person who stopped speaking is not the person best placed to fix a room that stopped listening. Returning the problem to her undoes most of six weeks.
choices.outcomenote: The worst, and the most tempting, because it is partly fair. Answering a question about your own delay by naming hers turns a moment of trust into a score being settled. She will keep contributing correctly and briefly, and she will never again ask you why something took as long as it did.

variants.situation:
The new format has held for six weeks. Priya raises things in the room again, and so does the new starter.

She catches you afterwards. "Can I ask something? For a while there it felt like the messages were the way to do it. I thought that was what you wanted."
variants.facilitatorspeech: I thought that was what you wanted.
variants.challenge: She is telling you what your agreement looked like from where she was standing. What do you say?

variants.situation:
The new format has held for six weeks. Priya raises things in the room again.

She catches you afterwards. "That first week - the cutover one. You were in that meeting too, weren't you?"
variants.facilitatorspeech: You were in that meeting too, weren't you?
variants.challenge: She is asking whether you watched it happen and said nothing. What do you say?

variants.situation:
The new format has held for six weeks. Priya raises things in the room again.

She catches you afterwards. "You caught me at my desk that first week, after the cutover meeting. Why not in the room?"
variants.challenge: She heard you. The team did not. What do you say?

variants.situation:
The new format has held for six weeks. Priya raises things in the room again.

She catches you afterwards. "You stopped that meeting for me in my first fortnight. I have been meaning to ask why it took another six weeks for anything to change."
variants.facilitatorspeech: Why did it take another six weeks?
variants.challenge: She is not complaining. She is asking a real question. What do you say?

nodes.title: She speaks, and the room waits
nodes.situation: Priya raises risks in the room now, and the team hears them in her voice. Dan is still fast, and has learned to leave a gap. Neither of those happened because someone tried harder; they happened because you changed what the meeting asked of them.
nodes.summary: You named what you observed rather than what you concluded, you gave Dan something he could act on, you refused a workaround that was quietly costing Priya her voice, and you put in place a structure that did not depend on anybody remembering to be good.

nodes.title: Better, and fragile
nodes.situation:
The stand-ups are better than they were. Priya contributes more than she did a month ago, though usually after you invite her, and Dan interrupts less when the agenda is light.

It holds while you are paying attention to it.
nodes.summary: You saw the problem and acted on it, which is more than most do. What is missing is a mechanism: most of what improved depends on you noticing, on Dan remembering, or on Priya finding it worth the effort — and each of those is the first thing a busy fortnight takes back.

nodes.title: The quietest person in the room
nodes.situation:
Priya's points reach the team through you, when they reach it at all. She is polite, productive and entirely disengaged from the meeting, and at her next review she asks what else is available.

The cutover incident is still in the retro document. Nobody connected it to the three unfinished sentences that preceded it.
nodes.summary: The information the team needed was in the room and had tried to reach you three times. What follows from not hearing it is rarely a dramatic failure — it is a capable person who stops trying, a decision made without the one fact that mattered, and a resignation that reads as unrelated.
